title: B-trees vs LSM trees
problem: An engine that rewrites whole pages for every small change cannot keep up with a write-heavy stream, and one that appends everything cannot answer reads without visiting many files.
summary: B-trees update fixed-size pages in place for predictable reads at the cost of random page writes; LSM trees append to a memtable, flush immutable SSTables and compact in the background, trading read and space amplification for sequential writes.
catTip: A B-tree is my food cupboard: every tin in its labelled place, tidy but fussy to restock. An LSM tree is me shoving each new toy under the sofa and sorting the pile at midnight.

recall.q: A key-value store ingests 200,000 sensor writes per second and serves occasional point lookups. Which structure fits, and what makes the lookups tolerable?
recall.a: An LSM tree: writes are sequential appends to a memtable that is flushed as SSTables. Bloom filters on each SSTable let a point lookup skip files that cannot hold the key, so reads touch few files despite the many levels.

guide.breaks: Pick a B-tree for a firehose of writes and random page rewrites saturate the disk; pick an LSM tree for a latency-sensitive read workload without tuning compaction and reads wander across many files while stalls appear at peak write load.
guide.tradeoffs: Every engine pays in some mix of read, write and space amplification: B-trees pay on writes, size-tiered LSM pays in space and reads, leveled LSM pays by rewriting data at every level.
guide.explainSimply: A B-tree is a filing cabinet: each change goes straight into its folder, so finding things is quick but filing is slow when folders fill up. An LSM tree is an inbox tray: everything lands on top instantly and gets sorted into bundles later. The tray is faster to fill; the cabinet is faster to search.
guide.hint: Ask whether the workload is dominated by writes or reads, then think about what keeps reads from checking every file.

meow: Memtable full? Flush to SSTable, compact at midnight. Bloom filter says not here and saves a paw-ful of reads.

quiz.prompt: In an LSM store a row was deleted, but after a replica that had been offline for three weeks rejoined, the row reappeared everywhere. What most likely happened?
options: Compaction removed the tombstone after gc_grace_seconds expired, before the lagging replica learned of the delete
A bloom filter returned a false negative
Leveled compaction merged the wrong level
quiz.explanation: A tombstone shadows older copies only while it exists; once compaction drops it, a replica still holding the old row re-propagates it as new data. Bloom filters never produce false negatives.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about amplification is correct?
options: Leveled compaction minimises write amplification and size-tiered minimises space amplification
B-trees have the lowest write amplification because each key is written once
Size-tiered compaction has low write amplification but higher read and space amplification; leveled compaction reverses that trade
quiz.explanation: Size-tiered rewrites data rarely but leaves duplicates across files; leveled keeps one copy per level at the cost of rewriting. B-trees write whole pages per change, so their per-row write amplification is high, not low.

cards.q: A RocksDB-backed service shows write latency spikes exactly during traffic peaks while disks are busy with background work. What is happening, and name two mitigations.
cards.a: Compaction debt: flushes and compactions cannot keep up, level 0 fills, and RocksDB throttles and then stops writes at its thresholds. Mitigations: give compaction more threads or I/O bandwidth, switch to universal (size-tiered) compaction to cut write amplification, or shed or buffer load upstream.

cards.q: Explain why a single B-tree insert can trigger writes to pages far apart on disk.
cards.a: The row goes into its leaf, every secondary index leaf for that row must be updated too, and a full leaf splits, pushing a separator into the parent. Each of those pages lives elsewhere on disk, so one logical insert becomes several random page writes.

glossary.note: An immutable file of key-value pairs in key order, written by flushing a memtable; the on-disk unit of an LSM tree.
